meta.title: Why craft-lovers are losing their craft
meta.author: hongminhee

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
Didn't the craft coders make other jobs redundant over the last 60 or so years?

I have vivid memories as a computer-loving kid having a family friend bitterly curse-out my fascination with these new devices -- because he was an old school architect and his inability to adapt to CAD had curtailed his career.

I want to be as compassionate as possible. I miss the craft as well, and there is grief there. These are real people and shift is jarringly rapid.

But I feel there is a real irony here that's being missed?

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
This one stings, and I think it's right.

Software engineers have spent decades building the infrastructure of automation. We told ourselves it was progress, and in some ways it was, but it also displaced a lot of people who didn't get to write think-pieces about craft and grief. The architect who cursed out your childhood fascination with computers had a point too.

Maybe there's something useful in this discomfort, though. If enough of us actually feel what it's like to have your livelihood threatened by a tool you didn't choose on terms you didn't set, that could build more solidarity with everyone else who's been through it already. Or we could just learn nothing and go back to not thinking about it once the immediate threat passes. History suggests the latter is more likely, but I'd rather not assume it.

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text:
Maybe there's something useful in this discomfort, though.


That’s a good lens. On that basis alone it's probably worth me sitting with this a bit longer.

Part of what makes this tricky for me is that my take on one level is self-serving. I use AI heavily, and I enjoy it. But equally I'm on the wrong side of this shift in a number of very material/real ways.

I think the thing that stands out to me is the rate of change. The right degree of it is energizing. Nobody really wants stasis, that would be boring. But this pace is different. It compresses the adjustment window in a way that’s hard to absorb, even if you're trying to lean into it like I am.

Perhaps seeing that - I wonder if it's a choice and I don't want to be in an eternal phase of grief?

comments.author: alexkorban
comments.text:
I think the rate of change is a useful thing to focus on. Alvin Toffler wrote about "future shock" created by the accelerating pace of change back in 1970. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Future_Shock

Some professions like software engineering got to ride the shockwave for a while instead of being dragged under, but now it's cresting over us as well.

comments.author: jonathannen
comments.text: Thanks! added to my reading queue.

comments.author: Kye
comments.text:
It took some bonus self-work to not lean heavily into the "that must be so hard for you (mockingly)" thing as coding career prospects vaporize in a Claude.

Graduated with a network admin degree (focus in Linux) just as the 2008 crash finished wiping out local IT in favor of the then-new cloud. At least the government paid for most of it, and my call to focus on Linux instead of taking the Cisco or Microsoft track on the theory that Linux would be more useful if it didn't lead to a job was right. The school switching from on-prem Outlook to web-based was an omen I didn't catch at the time.

comments.author: technomancy
comments.text:
If the grief Lawson describes is real (and I think it is), and if its deeper cause lies in the social relations around the technology rather than the technology itself, then the right target for that grief isn't the LLM coding assistant. It's whatever forces people to use tools they don't want to use, on terms they didn't choose.


This feels like a fallacy of assuming these are mutually exclusive. You can and should blame both!

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
Fair point, but I think the argument is less about blame and more about where change is actually possible. You can blame the hammer too, but the hammer doesn't change.

The reason I focus on the social relations is my own experience: same tools, different conditions (no employer, public funding), and the alienation just… isn't there. If the technology itself were the problem, that shouldn't work. So it seems like the more tractable target.

comments.author: james
comments.text: What does it even mean to blame a tool? Like how do you do that? Find one and shout at it?

comments.author: valpackett
comments.text:
All of this is 100% reasonable, but how can you ignore the ethical, moral, legal, social, and psychological concerns other than alienation?

For me, the entire business model of the corporations releasing these "assistants" would be reason enough to boycott them even if I wanted or liked having such "assistance".

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
Those concerns are real, and I don't want to wave them away. But I'd push back on one premise: that the current exploitative development model is the only possible one.

LLMs trained on publicly funded data, with open weights, by a cooperative or public institution rather than competing corporations, would still be LLMs. The technology doesn't require the business model. That's actually the argument I've been trying to make in a piece from earlier this year.

Boycotting current vendors makes sense on those grounds. I do think, though, that “boycott the technology” and “change who controls the technology” are different strategies with different long-term implications.

comments.author: mtset
comments.text: It is not the only possible one but it is the one we have right now. How do we change who controls the technology without boycotting the people who control it?

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
Fair, and I don't think boycott is useless, just incomplete on its own.

A few things that could work alongside or instead: legislative requirements that publicly funded research produce open-weight models, public procurement rules that push governments toward open alternatives, compute infrastructure treated as a public utility (the “CERN for AI” argument), or data cooperatives that give people collective bargaining power over training data.

The licensing route I've written about before (“TGPL”) is another angle. Not a silver bullet, but the point is there are multiple levers, and they work better together than any one of them alone.

comments.author: mtset
comments.text: I apologize if I missed it but I don't think your post addresses the fact that AI companies assert that copyright-based licensing simply doesn't apply to them at all. They consider their activities to be permitted under fair use, which means they can use GPL, MIT, and "TGPL" licenced software alike without recompense or attribution.

comments.author: natano
comments.text:
What always irks me about the fair use argument is, that there are many jurisdictions. An argument that might be correct for the U.S., might be wrong wherever I live. Who knows whether AI output is copyrightable, or whether training of an LLM is "fair use" in $COUNTRY.

Edit to clarify: Even if the AI was legally trained in the U.S., it might still have legal ramifications for users of the AI in other countries.

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
You're right that fair use is the main defense they're using, and it might hold up in court. But I don't think that makes licensing irrelevant, just not a standalone solution.

Licenses matter less as direct legal weapons right now and more as political and community signals. A “TGPL”-style license wouldn't immediately stop OpenAI, but it shifts the normative ground: it makes the extraction visible, names it as a violation of the spirit of open source, and gives future regulatory frameworks something to build on. GPL didn't work through constant litigation either; it worked by shaping expectations over time.

The fair use question also isn't fully settled. Some of the pending cases might go the other way. If they do, having clear license language in place already matters.

So yeah, licensing is one piece, not the whole answer. Which is why I listed it alongside regulatory and procurement approaches rather than treating it as sufficient on its own.

comments.author: Kye
comments.text: We need to figure that out quick since it seems like the disjointed half-decade long anti-AI movement is cooling to the point where it won't be directable toward effective political action soon. A boycott needs goals and teeth. I don't see much of either in the current situation, outside the deals Hollywood guilds got back in 2023 and are about to renegotiate from a position of strength bought by those AI provisions.

comments.author: intelfx
comments.text:
but how can you ignore the ethical, moral, legal, social, and psychological concerns other than alienation?


Just like that: *snaps fingers*

One is not required to fight or argue against all of the things all of the time. There is no legal or moral obligation to do so. Trying to induce outrage against anyone who has the gall to pick their battles in any direction other than yourself is, frankly, tiring. Especially the 1000th time around.

comments.author: mtset
comments.text:
It gives me a bitter chuckle to see this post - which is largely right, even if I don't agree (or even agree that Marx asserted) that smashing the looms was wrong - well-regarded on the same site where, right now, I'm being told that capitalism is the only viable economic system unless we come up with matter replicators.

If your plan to save the industry is to develop class consciousness among software engineers, you've already lost. Too many of us are permanently stuck in the mindset of the temporarily embarrassed millionaire.

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
That mindset exists, sure, mostly in the circles where Lobsters skews. I'm writing from Seoul, and it's much less dominant here than the comments section might suggest. Same goes for most of Europe, Latin America, and honestly most of the world where software engineers exist.

Treating “software engineers” as a monolithic class with uniform false consciousness is itself a bit Silicon Valley-centric. A lot of us are just workers. Not angling for a startup exit, not dreaming of stock options, just people who got into this because it was interesting and now need it to pay rent.

“Too many” having that mindset is different from “all of us do,” and the latter is what the argument would need.

comments.author: mtset
comments.text: I very much hope you're right. I currently work somewhere that is about as non-Silicon Valley as you can get in the US, and I still see the same problems with false consciousness - but I'd rather live in a world where programmers woke up to the reality of the situation, for sure.

comments.author: zem
comments.text: I continue to consider myself a craft coder even with the use of claude code. I can often roughly visualise up front the code that I want to produce, and either way I do examine every line that it generates, suggest (or sometimes manually perform) refactorings, etc, until I am happy with the code itself. it still feels like sculpting code into shape, versus targeting some output and not caring about how it is accomplished.

comments.author: tuxes
comments.text:
I have software preferences that aren't common in software (small programs; low dependency tree; integrates tightly with the platform; ...)

I experience a similar sense of craft at generating bespoke programs that adhere to those preferences.

It's not quite as strong a sense though. I don't think I'm in flow, which I miss.

comments.author: thev
comments.text:
We'll miss the feeling of holding code in our hands and molding it like clay in the caress of a master sculptor.



See, I have a problem with most talk around LLMs that is in the future tense. Folks are overwhelmed by how impressive this technology currently feels and then extrapolate it to an imagined future where it replaces them and the need to do any inspiring and pleasant work.

Both are not happening at this time though. You can't reliably let LLMs autonomously do all your work today. Sure, you may not need to do as much boilerplate work, but lovingly crafting optimized and maintainable code for a new algorithm or structure is not something an LLM can replace, not today, and that this will change is really not a given.

comments.author: technomancy
comments.text:
lovingly crafting optimized and maintainable code for a new algorithm or structure is not something an LLM can replace


The legitimate fear is not at all that an LLM can do it; it's that a CEO will get convinced that an LLM can do it. The hype doesn't have to be true to cause problems.

comments.author: thev
comments.text: From what I read, OP's fear is actually a future where an LLM can do it and I argue that the current situation does not imply this. That said, I do agree that the hype, even though it's not about reality, can definitely cause plenty of trouble.

comments.author: typesanitizer
comments.text: Off-topic: curious how you're handling writing in multiple languages? You're fluent and just translated by yourself? Or did you use machine translation (seems like the Japanese one is potentially LLM-translated from the Korean one?).

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
First off, I write everything in my native language, Korean. Then, I run it through a machine translator to get a rough draft. My go-to translator these days is Kagi Translate. After that, I review the translation and edit it until I'm happy with it. Next, I use an LLM to check my edits for any grammatical errors or awkward phrasing that might sound unnatural to a native speaker.

This workflow works pretty well for me because my English and Japanese skills are asymmetrical when it comes to reading and writing. I'm quite good at reading, but I struggle with writing.

comments.author: hsivonen
comments.text: Now that we are in the off-topic discussion about languages: This is the only time I’ve seen a choice of Hangul-only Korean and mixed-script Korean. I’m curious: Which one of these is the one you wrote first, and why are you offering the other variant?

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
I write in mixed-script Korean (國漢文混用體, hanja mixed with hangul) first, and that's the canonical version in my mind. There are two reasons I prefer it: I simply like hanja, and mixed-script does a much better job disambiguating homophones, which matters a lot for personal notes and searchability in tools like Obsidian.

The hangul-only version is generated automatically from the mixed-script source using a tool I wrote called Seonbi. I added it because most younger Koreans can't read mixed-script Korean fluently anymore; for many of them, the English version would actually be easier than the hanja-heavy one. So the hangul-only variant is essentially an accessibility affordance, even though I think of the mixed-script text as the real thing.

comments.author: xiaq
comments.text:
I adore the vertical layout you use for the Japanese and mixed-script Korean versions, it's beautiful to see even if I find it a bit harder to read compared to horizontal layout.

I'm Chinese and don't know any Korean at all, but whenever I read your article I always click on the Korean version to see which characters are used to translate technology concepts. Sometimes it's the same choice as in mainland Chinese, sometimes it's different, but it always fascinates me.

comments.author: hongminhee
comments.text:
Glad you enjoy the vertical layout; it felt like the natural choice for texts in that register.

Your habit of clicking over to the mixed-script version to check terminology is something I find genuinely delightful. Since you're interested in that kind of comparison, you might also enjoy a side project of mine: CJK computer science terms comparison, which systematically compares how programming and CS concepts are translated across mainland Chinese, Cantonese, Taiwanese Mandarin, Japanese, and Korean. The relationships between terms are often intricate. Take “recursion”: mainland and Taiwan share a character in 递/遞, Japan and Korea are effectively the same word in 再帰/再歸, and mainland, Japan, and Korea all converge on 归/帰/歸 for the second character, while Taiwan goes its own way with 迴.

comments.author: hsivonen
comments.text:
Thanks. I guess I’ll have to take a closer look at how Seonbi works. (The first thing I tried was U+F929 vs. U+6717 and they both resulted in the same Hangul in the South Korean mode but in different Hangul in the North Korean mode. This has interesting IME implications.)

(Previously, when I’ve been looking for this kind of mixed-script Korean that one assumes to find based on i18n materials, I’ve failed to find it either online or by looking around when traveling in South Korea, so it’s interesting to come across it when not looking for it.)

comments.author: davidcrespo
comments.text: That's so cool. I feel like you're living in the future in a way. You could see immediately even with early ChatGPT what LLMs would (eventually) do for translation. Seems like it still takes a bit of effort on your part to get a good result (and you're a high-skill user), which means it's not really ready for wide use.

comments.author: atmosx
comments.text: I am using a similar flow these days. I have not tested kagi translate, I will though (already paying customer). Thanks for sharing.

comments.author: kryptiskt
comments.text:
I think all the most important decisions in programming comes when coding in the small not when you're doing the overarching design, even when you're building a big system. The big design rarely contains anything novel and is mostly only a way to partition the work into pieces that is tractable to implement separately. Back in the 90s it was unfashionable to do the actual implementation work on these modules, the vision was that architects would give grunt programmers UML diagrams and that the implementation would be mechanical uncreative work. CASE tools such as Rational was a big deal.

There was a great resistance to these ideas at the time (read Joel on Software about architecture astronauts or The Pragmatic Programmer), and it turns out that the CASE visions were wrongheaded. In the same manner I think abdicating all the detail work to AI models are exactly as wrongheaded. The tactical decisions are the important decisions, and you can't build quality software without being involved with them.

comments.author: BinaryIgor
comments.text:
I don't now - for me the output is the value; if software doesn't provide one - whether it is optimization of some process, better access to information, new ability entirely - it is mostly worthless.

Also, LLMs change the process a little bit but not totally - we still need (and will) skills & knowledge to evaluate their output and guide them. What is more, there are many unknowns about sustainability of their use from multiple perspectives. And they are not automatically productivity boosters in all cases - sometimes they speed you up, sometimes they slow you down.

The article seems to extrapolate current situation into the future way too much.
